results.derivation_summary: Under §1692a(6), a "debt collector" is anyone whose business has the principal purpose of collecting debts, or who regularly collects debts "owed or due... another" — i.e., third-party collection — plus, for §1692f(6) purposes only, those whose principal business is enforcing security interests; the definition excludes creditors' own officers/employees, affiliated collectors, government officers, process servers, nonprofit credit counselors, and persons collecting debts they originated or that were not in default when obtained. A "creditor" (§1692a(4)) is one who extends credit or is owed the debt, excluding assignees who take a defaulted debt solely to collect for another, and a "debt" (§1692a(5)) is a consumer's obligation to pay money arising from a transaction primarily for personal, family, or household purposes. Henson confirms that a company collecting debts it purchased for its own account is not covered by the "owed another" prong (leaving the "principal purpose" prong unresolved), and Obduskey holds that a business doing no more than nonjudicial foreclosure is a debt collector only for §1692f(6). For notice/communication purposes, "consumer" is expanded by §1692c(d) and 12 C.F.R. §1006.6(a) to include the spouse, parent of a minor, guardian, executor/administrator, and (under Regulation F) a confirmed successor in interest.

results.derivation_summary: The FDCPA generally applies to a "debt collector," which is a person whose principal purpose is collecting debts or who regularly collects debts owed to another. The law covers the collection of "debts" arising from transactions for personal, family, or household purposes. A creditor collecting its own debt is generally not a debt collector, unless it uses a different name which implies a third-party is involved in the collection. A company collecting on debts it purchased for its own account is also not considered a debt collector under the "owed...another" definition.

edge_cases.scenario: A Florida homeowner is sued in a judicial foreclosure action by the servicer's law firm; the firm files the complaint, records a lis pendens, and sends the statutorily required notices, but never sends a validation notice and makes misrepresentations about the reinstatement amount in its pleadings. She asks whether the FDCPA applies to the foreclosure firm.
edge_cases.gap_description: The security-interest note and checklist item 7 frame the question as 'is the entity's role limited to enforcing a security interest (nonjudicial foreclosure, repossession) through steps required by state law?' A judicial-foreclosure firm literally answers 'yes' to the operative clause, routing it to '1692f(6) only -- no validation notice, no 1692e/1692f catalog.' Obduskey expressly confined itself to nonjudicial foreclosure, and lower courts (e.g., Glazer v. Chase Home Finance, 6th Cir.) hold judicial mortgage foreclosure IS debt collection and the firm is a fully covered debt collector. Roughly half the states are judicial-foreclosure states, so this misroute is common and materially wrong (it writes off validation-notice and false-representation claims).

edge_cases.scenario: A woman receives repeated calls and a letter from a collection agency about her ex-husband's (living) charged-off credit card. She never signed for the card, is not alleged to owe it, and the agency has disclosed the debt to her and to her employer's receptionist while trying to reach him. She asks whether the FDCPA gives her any rights.
edge_cases.gap_description: The gate's 'is it a debt / who is the consumer' items ask whether the contacted person is obligated or ALLEGEDLY obligated (1692a(3)), and checklist item 10 addresses non-obligors only in the deceased-obligor scenario. A non-obligor contacted about a LIVING person's debt answers 'no' to both and can be routed out of coverage, when in fact 1692b, 1692c(b), 1692d and 1692e protect 'any person' and she has an independent claim for the third-party disclosures. The node shows awareness of the third-party point only for estates, leaving the far more common wrong-number/skip-trace/relative-contact pattern unaddressed at the gate that all other FDCPA nodes depend on.

edge_cases.scenario: A borrower's mortgage servicing is transferred to a new servicer while she is 75 days delinquent but in an active COVID-era forbearance/trial modification plan; the note defines 'event of default' as acceleration after 90 days. The new servicer sends dunning letters with misstated amounts, and she asks whether it is a covered debt collector.
edge_cases.gap_description: Exclusion (F)(iii) is treated as dispositive on a binary 'was the debt in default when obtained,' but the node never defines 'default' and -- unlike 'regularly,' which it flags as contested -- gives no signal that this is the single most litigated element of mortgage-servicer FDCPA coverage (default is determined by the loan contract/state law, and delinquency, forbearance, or a trial plan is often not 'default'). A consumer who answers 'I was behind, so it was in default' will be told the servicer is covered when a court applying the note terms may hold it excluded (or vice versa), producing a materially wrong coverage conclusion for a very common servicing-transfer fact pattern.

results.derivation_summary: Under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a), an action on any contract, obligation, or liability founded on a written instrument must be brought within four years (the same four-year period applies under § 337(b) to book accounts, accounts stated in writing, and mutual open and current accounts, with the clock running from the date of the item or last item). Once that period has run, § 337(d) prohibits filing suit, arbitration, or any other proceeding to collect the debt, and the period may be extended only under § 360. Section 360 allows extension only by a written acknowledgment or promise signed by the party to be charged, or by a payment of principal or interest (which restarts the clock from the date of payment), but expressly provides that no payment alone revives a cause of action already barred. Other tolling that could apply on these facts includes emergency rule 9(a), which tolled limitations periods over 180 days from April 6, 2020 to October 1, 2020.

semantic_agreement_judge.agreement_notes: All three agree the limitations period for an action on a written contract in California is four years (Code Civ. Proc. § 337) and that once it runs, suit, arbitration, or other collection proceedings are barred. Analysis 1 is the most complete, adding the § 360 revival/tolling mechanics (written acknowledgment or payment, no revival of an already-barred claim), the § 337(b) account rules, and COVID-19 emergency rule 9(a) tolling; Analyses 2 and 3 simply omit these details without contradicting them.

diagnostics.manual_verification_note: Two independent reasons the live checker cannot verify this entry mechanically: (1) the previous url (www4.courts.ca.gov/documents/appendix-i.pdf) returns HTTP 403 to the checker on every run since 2026-09-02; (2) the rule exists only as a PDF and the checker has no PDF text extractor, so no courts.ca.gov url will ever substring-match. Url moved to the Judicial Council's own amendment order (courts.ca.gov/system/files/rules-court/20-05-28-rules-effective-20-05-29.pdf, 'Amendments to the California Rules of Court, adopted by the Judicial Council on May 28, 2020, effective May 29, 2020'), fetched and read in full 2026-09-04: rule 9(a) as amended reads 'Notwithstanding any other law, the statutes of limitations and repose for civil causes of action that exceed 180 days are tolled from April 6, 2020, until October 1, 2020.' (the PDF is a redline that also shows the struck original end-date language); 9(b) tolls periods of 180 days or less until August 3, 2020; the Advisory Committee Comment confirms the rule reaches limitations periods in codes other than the CCP. edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted in early 2021 on a Synchrony-issued store card (cardmember agreement designates Utah law, 6-year written-contract SOL) or a Citibank card (South Dakota law, 6 years). In 2026 the consumer asks whether a collection suit is time-barred; the node applies its 4-year period and reports the claim expired.
edge_cases.gap_description: The choice_of_law_note and the corresponding checklist item are written one-directionally: they contemplate an out-of-state clause only as a route to a SHORTER period (DE 3 years, Resurgence v. Chambers) and never flag that the same enforcement logic can import a LONGER foreign period (UT and SD are 6 years, VA 5). Synchrony (the largest retail-card issuer, Utah) and Citibank/Wells Fargo (South Dakota) agreements are the modal California card debts, so this is not a corner case. As encoded, the node tells such a consumer the debt is time-barred at 4 years when the creditor has a live 6-year argument under the very clause the node already tells the user to look for -- the dangerous direction (consumer does not answer, default judgment enters on a claim that was not clearly barred).

edge_cases.scenario: After defaulting on a credit card in 2019, the consumer signed a written payment/settlement agreement with a debt buyer in 2023 ('pay $75/month for 24 months and we'll settle for $3,000'), made four payments, and stopped in early 2024. The debt buyer sues in 2026 on the settlement agreement. The consumer asks whether the debt is time-barred.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node handles post-default payments only through the CCP 360 revival/acknowledgment frame (payment proviso limited to promissory notes; signed writing required to extend) and through the account-stated theory. It does not encode that a written settlement or workout agreement is itself a new written contract under 337(a) with its own accrual date running from breach OF THAT AGREEMENT -- so the node computes from the 2019 default, adds COVID tolling, and reports 'expired,' when the operative claim accrued in 2024 and is plainly live. Debt-buyer payment plans are extremely common, and the error runs in the dangerous direction (consumer told a live suit is barred and may not answer).

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer's home was sold at a nonjudicial trustee's sale in 2023; the sold-out junior lienholder on a HELOC (or a purchase-money second) now demands payment on the remaining balance, and the consumer asks whether the claim is time-barred.

results.derivation_summary: In Texas, a suit on a debt must be filed within four years after the cause of action accrues (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.004(a)(3)), and Tex. Fin. Code § 392.307(c) bars a debt buyer from suing or initiating arbitration on a consumer debt after that limitations period expires. Once the claim is time-barred under § 392.307(c), it is not revived by a payment, an oral or written reaffirmation, or any other activity on the debt, and under § 16.065 an acknowledgment of a stale claim is inadmissible to defeat limitations unless it is in writing and signed by the party to be charged. Limitations is an affirmative defense that the defendant must plead affirmatively under Tex. R. Civ. P. 94, or it may be lost. Separately, a rendered judgment goes dormant if no writ of execution issues within 10 years (§ 34.001) and may be revived within two years of dormancy, while foreign judgments are barred per § 16.066.
results.citation_used: Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.004(a); Tex. Fin. Code § 392.307(c)-(d); Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.065; Tex. R. Civ. P. 94

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted on a Capital One card in early 2020 (charge-off June 2020), then in 2022 signed a written payment-plan/settlement agreement with the collection agency acknowledging the balance and promising to pay, made three payments, and stopped. The debt buyer sued in late 2025 and the consumer wants to know if the claim is time-barred.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node screens only for payments made AFTER the 4-year period ran (no revival, 16.065 / 392.307), and its corrected accrual rule now fixes accrual at default/acceleration and ignores later activity entirely. It has no screen for a signed WRITTEN acknowledgment or new promise made DURING the period, which under CPRC 16.065 and Texas acknowledgment doctrine starts a new limitations period from the acknowledgment. The rule would report the 2025 suit as expired (accrual 2020 + 4) when it is likely timely -- the dangerous direction, and the mirror image of the fix already made in D-TX-SOL-CONSUMER-DEBT-02.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer stopped paying a defaulted federal Direct/FFEL student loan in 2016 and in 2025 receives a collection suit (or a demand from a guaranty agency/DOJ) and asks whether the Texas 4-year limitations period bars the claim.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's applies_to sweeps in all consumer debt on written or oral contract with no screen for federally-governed obligations. Federal student loans have no statute of limitations at all (20 U.S.C. 1091a expressly abolishes state and federal limitations for collection of such loans), and other U.S.-government contract debts run 6 years under 28 U.S.C. 2415. Applying the Texas 4-year period tells the consumer the claim is expired when it can never expire -- dangerous direction, and student-loan questions are among the most common consumer-debt inquiries.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer signed a promissory note for a personal loan (or an auto note that was accelerated after repossession) with a definite payment schedule; the lender accelerated in 2020 and the assignee sues on the note in 2025 for the deficiency.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node hard-codes a single 4-year period under CPRC 16.004 for all written-contract consumer debt. Actions to enforce a negotiable promissory note are governed instead by Tex. Bus. & Com. Code 3.118, which gives a six-year period running from the due date or acceleration. Texas courts apply 3.118 to notes, so a 2025 suit on a note accelerated in 2020 is timely; the encoded rule reports it expired -- the dangerous direction. Nothing in the logic or checklist asks whether the instrument is a promissory note rather than an account agreement.
